title: All things made for the rational creature
source_text: Ἐπεὶ ουν τούτοις πᾶσιν ἐπιφέρει ὁ Κέλσος τό· οὔκουν ἀνθρώπῳ πεποίηται τὰ πάντα, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ λέοντι οὐδὲ ἀετῷ οὐδὲ δελφῖνι, ἀλλ᾿ ὅπως ὅδε ὁ κόσμος ὡς ἂν θεοῦ ἔργον ὁλόκληρον καὶ τέλειον ἐξ ἁπάντων γένηται· τούτου χάριν μεμέτρηται τὰ πάντα, οὐκ ἀλλήλων ἀλλ᾿, εἰ μὴ πάρεργον, [ἀλλὰ] τοῦ ὅλου. καὶ μέλει τῷ θεῷ τοῦ ὅλου, καὶ τοῦτ᾿ οὔ ποτ᾿ ἀπολείπει πρόνοια, οὐδὲ κάκιον γίνεται, οὐδὲ διὰ χρόνου πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ὁ θεὸς ἐπιστρέφει, οὐδ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἕνεκα ὀργίζεται, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ πιθήκων οὐδὲ μυῶν· οὐδὲ τούτοις ἀπειλεῖ, ὧν ἕκαστον ἐν τῷ μέρει τὴν αὐτοῦ μοῖραν εἴληφε· φέρε κἂν διὰ βραχέων πρὸς ταῦτ᾿ ἀπαντήσωμεν. οἶμαι δὴ ἀποδεδειχέναι ἐκ τῶν προειρημένων, πῶς ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ παντὶ λογικῷ τὰ πάντα πεποίηται· προηγουμένως γὰρ διὰ τὸ λογικὸν ζῷον τὰ πάντα δεδημιούργηται. Κέλσος μὲν οὖν λεγέτω ὅτι οὕτως οὐκ ἀνθρώπῳ (ὡς) οὐδὲ λέοντι οὐδ᾿ οἷς ὀνομάζει· ἡμεῖς δ᾿ ἐροῦμεν· οὐ λέοντι ὁ δημιουργὸς οὐδ᾿ ἀετῷ οὐδὲ δελφῖνι ταῦτα πεποίηκεν, ἀλλὰ πάντα διὰ τὸ λογικὸν ζῷον, καὶ ὅπως [ἂν] ὅδε ὁ κόσμος ὡς ἂν θεοῦ ἔργον ὁλόκληρον καὶ τέλειον ἐξ ἁπάντων γένηται. τούτῳ γὰρ συγκαταθετέον (ὡς) καλῶς εἰρημένῳ. μέλει δὲ τῷ θεῷ οὐχ, ὡς Κέλσος οἴεται, μόνου τοῦ ὅλου ἀλλὰ παρὰ τὸ ὅλον ἐξαιρέτως παντὸς λογικοῦ. καὶ οὐδέ ποτε ἀπολείψει πρόνοια τὸ ὅλον· οἰκονομεῖ γὰρ, κἂν κάκιον γίνηται διὰ τὸ λογικὸν ἁμαρτάνον μέρος τι τοῦ ὅλου, καθάρσιον αὐτοῦ ποιεῖν καὶ διὰ χρόνου ἐπιστρέφειν τὸ ὅλον πρὸς ἑαυτόν. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ πιθήκων μὲν ἕνεκα ὀργίζεται οὐδὲ μυῶν· ἀνθρώποις δὲ ἐπάγει, ἅτε παραβᾶσι τὰς φυσικὰς ἀφορμὰς, δίκην καὶ κόλασιν, καὶ τούτοις διὰ προφητῶν ἀπειλεῖ καὶ διὰ τοῦ ἐπιδημήσαντος ὅλῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων σωτῆρος· ἵνα διὰ τῆς ἀπειλῆς ἐπιστραφῶσι μὲν οἱ ἀκούσαντες, οἱ δὲ ἀμελήσαντες τῶν ἐπιστρεπτικῶν λόγων δίκας κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τίσωσιν, ἃς πρέπον θεὸν ἐπιτιθέναι κατὰ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ συμφερόντως τῷ παντὶ βούλημα τοῖς τοιαύτης καὶ οὕτως ἐπιπόνου δεομένοις θεραπείας καὶ διορθώσεως. ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τοῦ τετάρτου τόμου αὐτάρκη περιγραφὴν εἰληφότος, αὐτοῦ που καταπαύσομεν τὸν λόγον. θεὸς δὲ δῴη διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, ὅς ἐστι θεὸς λόγος καὶ σοφία καὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ δικαιοσύνη καὶ πᾶν ὅ τι ποτὲ θεολογοῦσαι περὶ αὐτοῦ φασιν αἱ ἱεραὶ γραφαὶ, ἄρξασθαι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῖ πέμπτου τόμου ἐπ᾿ ὠφελείᾳ τῶν ἐντευξομένων καὶ διανύσαι κἀκεῖνον μετὰ τῆς τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν ψυχὴν ἐπιδημίας καλῶς.
pass_a_gloss: Since then (ἐπεί) to all these Celsus adds (ἐπιφέρω) this: 'Not therefore for man have all things been made (ποιέω), just as not for lion nor for eagle nor for dolphin, but so that this world (κόσμος), as being God's work (ἔργον), might become entire (ὁλόκληρος) and perfect (τέλειος) out of all; for the sake of this all things have been measured (μετρέω), not for one another but, except as a by-work (πάρεργον), [but] for the whole (ὅλος). And God has care (μέλει) for the whole, and providence (πρόνοια) never leaves (ἀπολείπω) this, nor does it become worse, nor does God through time turn (ἐπιστρέφω) to himself, nor is he angry (ὀργίζομαι) on account of men, just as not of apes (πίθηκος) nor of mice (μῦς); nor does he threaten (ἀπειλέω) these, of which each in its part has received (λαμβάνω) its own lot (μοῖρα).' Come, even if through brief words, let us meet (ἀπαντάω) these things. I think indeed I have demonstrated (ἀποδείκνυμι) from the things said before how for man and for every rational being (λογικός) all things have been made; for primarily (προηγουμένως) on account of the rational living being (ζῷον) all things have been crafted (δημιουργέω). Let Celsus then say that thus not for man, [as] not for lion nor for the ones he names; but we will say: not for lion did the Craftsman (δημιουργός) nor for eagle nor for dolphin make these things, but all things on account of the rational living being, and so that this world as God's work might become entire and perfect out of all. For to this one must assent (συγκατατίθεμαι) as well said. And God has care not, as Celsus thinks, of the whole only, but beyond (παρά) the whole especially (ἐξαιρέτως) of every rational being. And providence will never leave the whole; for he manages (οἰκονομέω), even if some part of the whole becomes worse on account of the rational being sinning (ἁμαρτάνω), to make a cleansing (καθάρσιον) of it and through time to turn the whole to himself. But neither on account of apes is he angry nor of mice; but on men, as having transgressed (παραβαίνω) the natural starting points (ἀφορμή), he brings (ἐπάγω) justice (δίκη) and punishment (κόλασις), and he threatens these through prophets and through the Saviour (σωτήρ) who sojourned (ἐπιδημέω) among the whole race of men; so that through the threat those who heard may turn, but those who neglected the turning words (ἐπιστρεπτικός) may pay penalties according to worth (ἀξία), which it is fitting for God to impose (ἐπιτίθημι) according to his own will (βούλημα), beneficially (συμφερόντως) for the all, on those needing such and so toilsome (ἐπίπονος) healing (θεραπεία) and correction (διόρθωσις). But since the fourth volume (τόμος) has taken a sufficient compass (περιγραφή), somewhere here we will stop (καταπαύω) the discourse. And may God give, through his Son, who is God Word and wisdom and truth and righteousness and whatever the holy scriptures, speaking as of God (θεολογέω) about him, say, that we begin also the fifth volume for the benefit (ὠφέλεια) of those who will read (ἐντυγχάνω), and complete (διανύω) that one also well with the sojourning (ἐπιδημία) of his Word into our soul.
pass_b_english: Since, then, Celsus adds to all this the words: “So all things have not been made for man, any more than for the lion, or the eagle, or the dolphin, but so that this world, as the work of God, might come to be whole and complete in all its parts. It is for this that all things have been measured out: not for one another, except incidentally, but for the whole. God cares for the whole, and providence never forsakes it; it does not grow worse, nor does God bring it back to himself after a time; nor is he angry on account of men, any more than on account of apes or mice; nor does he threaten these creatures, each of which has received its own lot in its place”, come, let us answer this, if only briefly.

I think I have shown from what was said earlier how all things have been made for man and for every rational being; for it is chiefly for the sake of the rational living being that all things have been created. So let Celsus say that things were not made for man, any more than for the lion or the other creatures he names. We, for our part, will say: the Creator did not make these things for the lion, or the eagle, or the dolphin, but made all things for the sake of the rational living being, and “so that this world, as the work of God, might come to be whole and complete in all its parts.” For we must agree with this, since it is well said. God cares, not, as Celsus thinks, for the whole alone, but beyond the whole, and in a special way, for every rational being. And providence will never forsake the whole. For even if some part of the whole grows worse because the rational being sins, God so orders things as to make a cleansing of it and, in time, to turn the whole back to himself. Nor indeed is he angry on account of apes or mice; but on men, because they have transgressed the starting points that nature gave them, he brings retribution and punishment. These he threatens through the prophets and through the Saviour who came to dwell among the whole human race, so that through the threat those who hear may turn, while those who neglect the words that call them to turn may pay the penalty they deserve. It is fitting for God to impose such penalties, according to his own will and for the good of the whole, on those who need healing and correction of this kind, and so painful.

But since this fourth book has now reached a sufficient length, we will bring our discourse to a close about here. May God grant, through his Son, who is God the Word (John 1:1), and Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Truth (John 14:6), and Righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and whatever else the sacred Scriptures say of him when they speak of him as God, that we may begin the fifth book also, for the benefit of those who will read it, and bring it too to a good end, with his Word coming to dwell in our soul.

choices.term: οὐδὲ διὰ χρόνου πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ὁ θεὸς ἐπιστρέφει
choices.english: nor does God bring it back to himself after a time
choices.why: Celsus's clause has no object; 'it' (the whole) is supplied from Origen's reply, where God turns τὸ ὅλον back to himself διὰ χρόνου. Celsus is denying what Origen then affirms.
rejected: nor does God turn back to himself after a time

choices.english: God so orders things as to make a cleansing of it and, in time, to turn the whole back to himself
choices.why: The subject of οἰκονομεῖ is unexpressed; masculine ἑαυτόν points to God (from μέλει τῷ θεῷ), not to feminine πρόνοια, so 'God' is supplied.
rejected: providence orders things ... back to itself

choices.english: because they have transgressed the starting points that nature gave them
choices.why: ἀφορμαί are the natural resources or starting points given to the rational creature; 'starting points' keeps the word without adding a doctrine of virtue that the clause does not state.

choices.term: ὅς ἐστι θεὸς λόγος καὶ σοφία καὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ δικαιοσύνη
choices.english: who is God the Word, and Wisdom, and Truth, and Righteousness
choices.why: Titles of the Son drawn from Scripture; capitalised as names of the Son under house style, with inline citations to the verses that give them.
rejected: who is God, word and wisdom and truth and righteousness

choices.english: when they speak of him as God
choices.why: θεολογέω here is 'to speak of someone as God' (the Scriptures' titles for the Son), not 'to do theology'.

choices.term: οὔκουν, οὐδὲ ... οὐδὲ, οὔ ποτ᾿, οὐδὲ κάκιον, οὐδ᾿ ... ὀργίζεται, οὐδὲ ... ἀπειλεῖ
choices.choice: Second pass: negations in Celsus's string (οὔκουν, οὐδὲ ... οὐδὲ, οὔ ποτ᾿, οὐδὲ κάκιον, οὐδ᾿ ... ὀργίζεται, οὐδὲ ... ἀπειλεῖ) all kept; Origen's reply affirms the same points in the same order (cares beyond the whole, providence will never forsake, God turns the whole back in time, anger and threats aimed at men).

Second pass: ἵνα clause keeps both outcomes (those who hear turn; those who neglect pay the deserved penalty) and ἃς πρέπον θεὸν ἐπιτιθέναι is split into its own sentence ('It is fitting for God to impose such penalties ...'); no claim added or dropped.
Second pass: Scripture titles checked against John 1:1 (θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος), 1 Corinthians 1:24 (θεοῦ σοφίαν), John 14:6 (ἡ ἀλήθεια), 1 Corinthians 1:30 (σοφία ... δικαιοσύνη).

Source: Perseus TEI (Koetschau GCS 2, pp. 372-374), chapter 4.99; the staged source_4.json stopped at 4.98, so this chapter was taken from the TEI and translated from the Greek on 2026-10-24. The TEI's bracketed [ἀλλὰ] and [ἂν] are Koetschau's deletions and are not translated; the supplements (ὡς) are read. The TEI misprints 'ουν' (for οὖν) and 'τοῖ πέμπτου' (for τοῦ πέμπτου); both are read in the obvious sense and left as printed in the source row. Celsus's words are in double quotation marks; Origen re-quotes his phrase 'so that this world ... in all its parts' in the second paragraph and agrees with it. The phrase ὁλόκληρον καὶ τέλειον ἐξ ἁπάντων may echo Plato, Timaeus 32c-33a (a world whole and complete from complete parts); not certain, so no inline citation. The titles of the Son in the closing prayer are cited inline: God the Word (John 1:1), Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), Truth (John 14:6), Righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30); Wisdom and Righteousness also stand together in 1 Corinthians 1:30. 'book' renders τόμος (volume) as elsewhere in this translation.
